book.title: Maaser Sheni
book.sourceNote: Sefaria Community Translation; Sefaria public export. CC0 · Sefaria Community Translation; public-domain dedication where that selected English version is available.

1.text: Second tithe [produce]: One may not sell it, use it as collateral, pawn it, exchange it, or weigh gold dinars against it, even in order to deconsecrate other second tithe produce on their behalf. Nor may one given them to a moneychanger or use them to create a good impression (i.e., of one's business), to repay a debt, or to make oneself appear wealthy* להתעשר not להתעטר ("to crown oneself") (GR"A); alt., להתגדל ("to make oneself appear great") (Rambam); see discussion in Lieberman here through them. If it is so that they will not become moldy, behold, that is permitted.

How so, "one may not sell it"? One should not say to another, "Take two hundred and give me a maneh." How so, "one may not use it as collateral"? One should not enter [a debtor's] house and take his second tithe [produce] as collateral. How so, "one may not pawn it"? One should not say to another, "Take this tithe and it let it stay in your possession, and give me unconsecrated [produce] on its behalf." How so, "one may not exchange it"? One should not say to another, "Take this wine and give me that oil," [or] "Take this oil and give me that wine." Rather, one says to him, "Take this wine because I don't have oil," and the other says to him, "Take this oil because I don't have wine." It comes out that they have exchanged [in fact] but they have not exchanged [contractually], and each one does a favor to the other.
Second tithe [produce] may not be applied to a rash or to a callous, nor may it be made into an amulet.

They may not redeem second tithe [produce] with uncoined metal (Maaser Sheni 1:2), but Rabbi Dosa permits it. But small coins bearing the insignia of a bathhouse (i.e., used as tender for entry to a public bathhouse) -- all agree that they may not redeem it with them.

They may not redeem it either with coins of the rebellion,*מרוד not מדור, see GR"A, MSS or with uncirculated coins, or with money that is not in one's possession. How so? If he had Kozibian money (i.e., coins minted following the Bar Kochba (Koziba) revolt)*This appears to be the only direct mention of Bar Kochba in the Tosefta, and there are no direct mentions in the Mishna. or Jerusalem money, they may not redeem it with them (i.e., those coins). If it was [nonetheless] redeemed, they may not purchase tithe with them, but [as to] coins circulated by the early kings, they may redeem it for them. They may not redeem it either with money from here*של כאן=שכן (see Lieberman) that is in Babylonia, nor with [Babylonian] money that is in Babylonia, but if he was here and he had money from Babylonia, they may redeem it with them. How so, "They may not redeem [second tithe] with money that is not in his possession"? If he had money in a camp*קצטרא not קיסטרא (=tin), see Lieberman; alt., קיסטרא (=a large, unwieldy vessel), see GR"A; alt., קסטרא (=Castra, a locale), see Minchat Yitzchak. Despite the uncertainty re: the exact wording, the unifying idea is that the money is not presently available or accessible. or in the King's hill country*בהר המלך not בית המלך ("palace") (Lieberman; MS Erfurt), or that fell from his purse into a pit -- even if he knows that it's there, they may not redeem it with them, and if it was [nonetheless] redeemed, he may not purchase tithe [with that money].

Similarly, one who comes along the road with coins in his hand, and he sees a robber coming toward him: He should not say, "Behold, these are hereby deconsecrated on account for the coins that I have inside my house." [However,] if he did so, his words stand. [If] he was laden with jugs of wine or jugs of oil and saw that they were breaking, he should not say, "Behold, these are hereby designated as terumah and tithes on behalf of the produce that I have inside my house." If he he did so, behold, that is forbidden.

One may purchase wild animals and fowl [in Jerusalem] for "meat for one's craving" (see Deut. 12:20 and Deut. 14:26), but not for peace offerings. From the time that they decreed that "meat for one's craving" defiles the hands, they said, one may not purchase a wild animal for "meat for one's craving," but one may purchase fowl for "meat for one's craving." Rabbi Elazar ben Yehuda, a man from Avlin (אבלין) says, one also cannot [purchase] fowl for "meat for one's craving," since all the wine-pressing is done on top of "meat for one's craving" that is impure vis-a-vis consecration and pure (alt., "impure," Lieberman) for terumah.

One who purchases an open jug in Jerusalem needs to consume the equivalent value of the storage vessel*מרוד (see Bartenura to Maaser Sheni 1:3); sealed, there is no need to consume the equivalent [value] of the storage vessel. When do these words apply? With regards to wine; however, with regards to [jugs of] vinegar brine, or fish brine, or oil, or honey, whether open or sealed, there is no need to consume the equivalent value of the storage vessel.

Early-stage date pomace and late-stage date pomace: One need not consume their equivalent value. If there were [in] baskets, behold, one consumes [the equivalent value]. And as to all other matter, one need not eat the equivalent value: Not the equivalent of grape-shell pomace, and not the equivalent value of grape-flesh pomace, and not the equivalent value of olive waste.
One who purchases a deer in Jerusalem need not consume the equivalent value of the hide. [If it was] slaughtered, one must consume the equivalent value of the hide.

They may not lease out houses in Jerusalem because they belong to the tribes. Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon (alt., "b'Rabbi Tzadok") says, not even the beds. [Therefore, with regards to] the hides of sacrificial offerings [used in lieu of payment for lodging], the innkeepers [are considered to] have come and taken them by force (see Meg. 26a:15).

Young shoots of hawthorn and carob, before they sweeten, may not be purchased with [second] tithe money. Once they sweeten, they may be purchased with [second] tithe money, but luf (see Tosefta Sheviit 4:2), and mustard, and lupine, and all other pickled [produce], whether they have sweetened, or whether they have not yet sweetened, may be purchased with [second] tithe money.

Young safflower*alt., חלות חריע ("loaves of safflower," as below) (GR"A; see Mishnah Oktzin 3:5); alt., הריע (Lieberman) may be purchased with second tithe money, and they do not defile with food-impurity. Loaves of safflower: Said Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri came to the place of Rabbi Chalafta. He said to him, "Loaves of safflower, what is their status -- may they be purchased with second tithe money?" He said to him, "They may not be purchased." He said to him, "Even I say so. However, Akiva says that they may be purchased."

A heart of palm may be purchased with [second] tithe money, and does not defile with food-impurity. And unripe dates may be purchased with [second] tithe money, and they do defile with food-impurity. Rabbi Yehuda says, [with respect to] a heart of palm, behold, it is like wood in every respect except that it may be purchased with [second] tithe money; [and] unripe dates, behold, they are like fruits in every respect, except that they are exempt from tithes. Rabbi Shimon says in the name of Rabbi Eliezer, turmeric may not be purchased with [second] tithe money because it has no taste, [and is only useful] for the sake of its appearance (i.e., to use as a dye). Said Rabbi Yehuda ben Garush (alt., "Gadish") before Rabbi Eliezer: "Those of the house of my father would sell brine in Jerusalem." [Rabbi Eliezer said,] "That is no proof, lest the fish [from which the brine was concocted] were sold along with it."

One who purchases an animal [with second tithe money outside of Jerusalem*see Minchat Bikkurim; Maaser Sheni 1:6] to sacrifice as a peace offering: [If the purchase was] inadvertent*e.g., the purchaser didn't know he was using second tithe money to buy the animal, the purchase price is restored to its [former] place (i.e., to the purchaser); [if] intentional, he ascends and it is consumed in its [chosen] place (i.e., the Holy Temple). In these days, [the animal is left] to die. Said Rabbi Yehuda, when do these words apply? Whenever one intended to purchase [the animal] ab initio for the sake of being a peace offering, but if he intended to spend second tithe money for [an animal designated for] non-sacrificial use, whether inadvertent or intentional, the purchase price is restored to its [former] place. If they were impure fruits, whether inadvertent or intentional, the purchase price is restored to its [former] place.

A log of [second tithe] wine that fell inside a log of [unconsecrated] honey, and behold, there are are [now] two logs, the increase in value [is divided] according to the proportion (see Maaser Sheni 2:5). A cooked dish of second tithe that was spiced with unconsecrated spices, the increase in value [is divided] according to the proportion. And [a cooked dish] of unconsecrated [produce] that was spiced with second tithe spices, the second tithe [portion] cannot escape redemption. Second tithe leeks and unconsecrated [leeks] that were spiced together*שניתבלו; alt., שנתבשלו ("that were cooked [together]") (GR"A), the increase in value [is divided] according to the proportion.

[If] he had dough of second tithe and he baked it, the increase in value [is divided] according to the proportion. [If] the bread fell apart, or the cooked dish got burnt, the loss in value [is attributed] to second [tithe]. One who sorts wheat, or grinds it, or sifts it: Its redemption price is like any other wheat. Rabbi Yosei says, in a place where they calculate their expense, they may redeem the wheat, but they may not redeem the [baked] loaves; [and] in a place where they do not calculate their expense, they may even redeem the loaves.

Second tithe oil and unconsecrated choice perfumes*ראשי בשמים (see Songs 4:14) that got mixed, the increase in value [is measured] according to the proportion. This is the general rule: Said Rabbi Yosei, whatever increases in measure [as a result of being mixed with unconsecrated produce], [if] the improvement [in value] can be recognized, the improvement [is calculated] according to the proportion, [and] whatever does not increase in measure, [if] the improvement [in value] can be recognized, the [entire] improvement [goes] to second tithe (see Maaser Sheni 2.1).

2.text: [With respect to] fenugreek of terumah that the daughter of a priest used to rub onto her head [as a perfume], the daughter of an Israelite has no right to rub it [on her own head] afterwards, but she may rub her hair together with the hair [of the daughter of a priest].

Fenugreek of [second] tithe may [only] be eaten when it is tender. [Fenugreek] of terumah: Beit Shammai say, anything done with it must be done in purity, and Beit Hillel say, anything done with it must be done in purity, except for cleansing the head, the words of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda says, Beit Shammai say, anything done with it must be done in purity, except for cleansing the head, and Beit Hillel say, anything done with it must be done in purity, except for soaking it in water. (See Maaser Sheni 2:3 (following Rabbi Yehuda's view).)

Vetches of second tithe may [only] be eaten when they are tender. [Vetches] of terumah: Beit Shammai say, they must be soaked in purity, but they can be rubbed and given for food in impurity, and Beit Hillel say, they must be soaked and rubbed in purity, but they can be given for food in impurity, the words of Rabbi Yehuda.*Compare Maaser Sheni 2:4 and Eduyot 1:8 (switching the positions). Rabbi Meir says, Beit Shammai say, they must be soaked and rubbed in purity, and Beit Hillel say, anything done with them must be done in purity. Said Rabbi Yosei, that is the mishnah (teaching) of Rabbi Akiva. Therefore, he says, they may be given to any priest, but the Sages did not agree with him (see Hallah 4:9).

They may not soak dates to produce date-beer from them, nor raisins to produce raisin-juice, but they may be crushed into terrima ("a drink or brew prepared of pounded groats and spices" (Jastrow)). [However, all] this may be done with spices, because that is their [normal] preparation. One may bind up spices and place [the bundle] inside a cooked dish; if their flavor is nullified, they are permitted, and if not, they are forbidden.

They may not make aluntit wine (see Tos. Terumot 9:8) or spiced oil [using second tithe produce]. One may rub oil [on one's body] but one may not rub wine or vinegar [on one's body], for it is the nature of oil to be rubbed, but it is not the nature of wine or vinegar to be rubbed.

Unconsecrated coins and consecrated coins that were scattered [and intermingled], that which one collects is collected for consecration (i.e., for the Temple treasury). It is the same [rule] for coins [intermingled] with coins, produce with produce, pomegranates with pomegranates, and anything whose nature is to become mixed up (i.e., such that one is indistinguishable from the other), but something whose nature is not to become mixed up, that which one collects is collected for both purposes, and that which is left behind is left behind for both purposes.

A selah of second tithe and of unconsecrated status that got mixed up: One purchases copper coins in exchange for the selah. Ben Azzai says, two selah's worth [of coins]. An unconsecrated selah and a consecrated [selah] that got mixed up: One chooses the finer one between them and says, "If this one is consecrated, behold, it is consecrated, and if not it is consecrated regardless, for this one may be exchanged for that one." And the second one, behold, it is permitted [for common use]. § A selah of second tithe and of consecrated status that got mixed up: One purchases copper coins in exchange for the selah, and says, "[This is] a selah of second tithe regardless, for it may be exchanged for these copper coins." [Then] he chooses the finer one between them and says, "If this one is consecrated, behold, it is consecrated, and if not it is consecrated regardless, for this one may be exchanged for that one." [Then] he takes the second one and exchanges the copper coins on its behalf.Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon says, "Just as they may exchange silver for copper, so too may they exchange gold for silver." Rebbi said to him, "And why do they exchange silver for copper? For in the same way they may exchange silver for gold. [But] gold may not be exchanged for silver, for they do not exchange gold for copper." Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon says, they may exchange second tithe golden [coins] for copper coins that are in Jerusalem. When do these words apply? With regard to demai, but with regard to certainly untithed produce, behold, that is forbidden. But with demai, they may exchange it food for food. Second tithe of gold that was made into vessels may not be redeemed. If it was made of silver, behold, that is permitted. Second tithe of demai that got mixed up with that of certainly untithed produce: They are eaten with the stringencies of both of them.

Second tithe of gold that they fashioned into vessels may not be redeemed. If it was of silver, behold, that is permitted. Second tithe of demai that was mixed together with that of certainly tithed produce: They are eaten according to the stringencies of both of them.

There is a stringency in consecrated items that there is not in second tithe, and in second tithe that there is not in consecrated items. Consecrated items may all be exchanged for one another, [but] second tithe may only be exchanged for money. Consecrated items do not change their level of sanctity, [but] second tithe's sanctity can increase after consecration (see Lieberman). Consecrated items are brought into Jerusalem and taken out of Jerusalem, [but] second tithe is brought into Jerusalem but is not taken out of Jerusalem. The stringency with second tithe over consecrated items is that second-tithe may acquire jars of wine (Maaser Sheni 1:3), but its money is forbidden, a doubtful admixture of any quantity is forbidden, and one is required to add a fifth (see Maaser Sheni 4:3), and is required to make a confession (Maaser Sheni 5:10), and it is forbidden to mourners (Maaser Sheni 5:12), and one is only permitted to eat it if it has been redeemed (Maaser Sheni 3:6), and one may not use it to kindle a candle, which is not the case with consecrated items. The stringency with consecrated items is that consecration takes effect on all items, and one is prohibited to derive personal benefit from it, and one is only permitted to eat it if it has been redeemed, which is not the case with second tithe.

Rabbi Meir says, they may not exchange silver and produce on behalf of silver unless he has with him an itemized account [of the money and of the value of the produce], and the Sages permit it (Maaser Sheni 2:8). Rabbi Ya'akov says in his name, three dinars of silver, and a dinar's worth of five copper coins and five fruits. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says, Shammai the Elder says, he sets them down in a store and consumes their equivalent value.

[If] he had two storerooms, one for terumah and one for second tithe, and he found produce between them: [If it was] closer to the terumah, it falls to terumah; to second tithe, it falls to second tithe; half-and-half, both stringencies are imposed upon him. Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda says, [if there was] a chest that had been used for unconsecrated and second-tithe [coins], and he found coins [of unknown status] inside it: If the majority [of people] placed unconsecrated [coins] inside of it, [they are all considered] unconsecrated. If the majority placed second tithe [coins] inside of it, [they are all considered] second tithe. Rabbi Shimon said to them, behold, [this situation is similar to] peace offerings that [still] have the breast and thigh (see Lev. 7:30-34), which are forbidden to non-priests, [as to which the law is lenient (see Maaser Sheni 3:2)]. Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Yosei, thus said Beit Hillel to Beit Shammai, "If you concede regarding produce whose processing has not been completed, that if one redeems second tithe, he may not eat it in any place, [then you must concede the same] even as to produce whose processing has been completed."*The following translation follows Lieberman. Beit Shammai said to them, "No. If you hold that regarding produce whose processing has not been completed, that one may redeem them to remove them from being subject to terumah and tithe, [then you must hold the same as to produce whose processing has been completed]." Beit Hillel said to them, "Even produce whose processing has been completed can be made into terumah and tithes on behalf of [produce in] another location." Another version: One is only liable for terumah and tithes before he has set aside [a portion as] terumah.

A tree that is standing inside (i.e., within the boundaries of Jerusalem), and its branches spread outside: Its second tithe may be redeemed. [If one] turned its branches back inside, its second tithe may not be redeemed. [If] it was standing outside, and its branches spread inside, its second tithe may not be redeemed. [If one] turned its branches back outside, its second tithe may be redeemed.

Houses whose entrances are within [the walls of Jerusalem] and their inner space is outside, [or] their entrances are outside and their inner space is within: Beit Shammai say, they may not redeem second tithe in them as though they are [fully] within, and they may not eat offerings of lesser sanctity in them as though they are [fully] outside. And Beit Hillel say, that which corresponds to (i.e., is on the same plane as) the wall [of Jerusalem] and within [is treated] like it is inside, and that which corresponds to the wall and outside [is treated] like it is outside. Said Rabbi Yosei, this is [the language of the] Mishnah of Rabbi Akiva. [However, according to the language of] the first Mishnah, Beit Shammai say, they may not redeem second tithe in them as though they are [fully] within, and they may not eat offerings of lesser sanctity in them as though they are [fully] outside, and Beit Hillel say, behold, they are [considered to be] like the Temple chambers: Those facing (lit., "whose lips are") inside are [considered to be] inside, and those facing outside are considered to be outside.

A chamber that was built in a holy area and opened into a profane area, [or] within a profane area and its roof [is within] a holy area, they may not eat*אין אוכלין (MS Erfurt; GR"A) most holy foods in it, and they may not slaughter sacrifices of lesser sanctity in it, and they are not liable for impurity on account of it. [If it was] built in a profane area and opened into a holy area: Even though they may not keep it that way, its interior space is holy and its roof is profane. They may eat most holy sacrifices in it, and they may slaughter sacrifices of lesser holiness in it, and they are liable for impurity on account of it. [If] it was built in a holy area and opened into [both] a profane area and a holy area, all of it is holy. [If] it was built in a profane area and opened into [both] a holy and a profane area, all of it is profane. [If] it was built in [both] a holy and a profane area, and opened into [both] a holy and a profane area, such as the Chamber of the Hearth, their interior space and their roofs that face the holy, and [that extend] into the holy, are holy, and that which faces the profane and [extends] into the profane is profane. If [the question involves] the consumption of sacrifices, everything follows after the [location of] the entrance. If [the question involves] a matter of impurity [in an area] that faces the wall and within*note that MS Erfurt omits the phrase "that faces the wall and within", everything follows after the entrance.

[If] it was built into the wall of Jerusalem, they may eat most holy offerings in it, but they may not slaughter offerings of lesser sanctity in it. [If] it was built into the wall of the woman's courtyard, they may slaughter offerings of lesser sanctity in it, but they may not redeem second tithe in it.
A house that is built into a wall: Rabbi Yehuda says, it is [treated] as though it is outside [the wall]. Rabbi Shimon says, it is [treated] as though it is within [the wall].

[In regards to] all the chambers, all of them are [considered to be] built in the Temple. Rabbi Yosei says, the boundaries of the Land of Israel that are [referenced] in Scripture are adjudged like outside the Land. Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Yosei says, they are adjudged like the Land of Israel.

3.text: One who carries second tithe produce from an expensive place to a cheap place, or from a cheap place to an expensive place, redeems it according to the market price of the place [of redemption] (Maaser Sheni 4:1). Said Rabbi Yehoshua ben Karcha, when do these words apply? In regards to demai, but in regards to certainly tithed [produce], they redeem it according to the market price of the cheap place.

They redeem second tithe according to the cheap market price, like [the market price that] the moneychanger purchases at but not like [the market price that] he sells at. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says, like the [market price at which] the moneychanger purchases the same type.

Second tithe whose value is not known may be redeemed by the testimony of three [expert] purchasers, but not on the testimony of three who are not [expert] purchasers, even if one is of them is a non-Jew and even if one of them is the owner. They may force the owner to make the first bid. [But] if he said, "I will acquire it for an issar," he may retract [his acceptance if it is deemed unreasonable]. This is a stringency of dedicated items [wherein one may not retract] over second tithe.

Second tithe may not be redeemed by estimation; rather, by [a precise estimate of the] value. How so? [If] he had rotten produce or corroded coins, one should not say, "How much is a person willing to pay for this collection?" or "How much is one willing to pay for this pile?" Rather, he says, "How much of this produce (פירות), see Lieberman) is one willing to purchase with a sela?" or "How many of these coins is one willing to purchase with a dinar?"

One who sells fruits to his fellow: [If] the seller says, "I sold untithed produce to you," and the buyer says, "You sold me tithed produce," they force the seller to tithe his own produce [on account of that which he sold]. Behold, if they sold [the produce from] the threshing floor of the king's house: If it was due to an obligation, he needs to tithe on his behalf. If it was due to coercion, he does not need to tithe on his behalf.

One who eats tithed produce, whether inadvertently or intentionally, should appeal to Heaven, the words of Rebbi. Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel says, inadvertently he should appeal to Heaven; intentionally he should return the value [of what was eaten] to their place.

One who eats the untithed produce of his fellow must repay him the price of the tithes [within] the untithed produce, the words of Rebbi. Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda says, the price of the unconsecrated produce within it.

One who brings produced from the threshing floor to the city, one who separated terumah and gave it to a priest, first tithe and gave it to a Levite, and poor-tithe and gave it to a poor person may not deduct from them the price of transporting [the produce], but if he designated it [specifically] for them in the threshing floor, he may deduct from them the price of transporting it.

One who sells produce to his fellow and says to him, "The produce that I sold to you is untithed," [or] "This is the meat of a first-born animal," [or] "This is wine of libation," then what they ate, they ate, and [the seller] should return the purchase price to them. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says, [if the item sold is] something from which one is repulsed, then what they ate, they ate, and he must return the remainder to them. But something that one is not repulsed from, what they ate, they ate, and he ate, and he deducts the value for them (i.e., he deducts the value of the benefit and reimburses them the balance).

They may not redeem second tithe in Jerusalem at this time (i.e., after the destruction), and they may not separate second tithe in Jerusalem at this time, and they may not deconsecrate second tithe in Jerusalem at this time, and they may not sell second tithe in Jerusalem at this time, and they may not take second tithe out of Jerusalem in this time, and if they took it out, it should be left to rot. [But] they may deconsecrate coins on behalf of produce in Jerusalem in this time. Beit Shammai say, both of them (i.e., the coins and the produce) are considered second tithe, and Beit Hilel say, the coins return to their former status, and the produce returns to its former status.

Beit Hillel say, a person may separate first tithe of demai, and separate its terumah, and eat it, and there is no need to separate second [tithe]. Beit Shammai say, one needs to separate second [tithe]. One who separates the terumah of second [tithe must also] separate the terumah of first [tithe]. One who separates the terumah of first [tithe] need not separate the terumah of second [tithe]. And the halacha is according to the words of Beit Shammai.

[If] he saw someone who separated second tithe, he is believed [to have also separated] first [tithe], the words of Rabbi Eliezer. And the Sages say, [if] he is believed about first [tithe], he is believed about second [tithe], [and if] he is not believed about second [tithe], he is not believed about first [tithe].

[If] he separated terumah, and first tithe, and second tithe, and ate them: On behalf of the same species, he is believed; on behalf of a different species, he is not believed, the words of Rabbi Eliezer. And the Sages say, even on behalf of the same species, he is not believed. For he does not have the right to fix his own [tithes] and come and ruin ours.

4.text: One who redeems his own second tithe, behold, he is liable for the one-fifth penalty. It is the same if one enters within his own, or purchases from a Samaritan or from a non-Jew.

They may act deceptively in regards to second tithe (Maaser Sheni 4:4), in order to exempt it from the one-fifth [penalty]. How so? A person may say to his adult son or daughter, to his Hebrew slave or maidservant, "Take these coins and redeem this tithe with them." But he may not say to him [or her], "Redeem for me this tithe with them." Said Rabbi Yehoshua ben Karcha, originally they were accustomed to doing so, [but] once swindlers proliferated, [the Sages instituted that] a person may say to his fellow, "Behold, these fruits are given to you as a gift," and he returns and says to him, "Behold, these are hereby exchanged on behalf of fruits that I have in my house" -- as long as he does not say, "Behold, these are hereby exchanged on behalf of coins that I have inside my purse" -- unless the homeowner has [already] transferred [the fruits] into his hand, or unless he has [already] leased his place (i.e., where the produce is located) to him.

[In the case of] two brothers, or two business partners, or a father and his son — they may redeem each other's second tithe [ma'aser sheni] and give each other the tithe for the poor. Rabbi Yehudah said, "A curse should come to one who gives the tithe for the poor to his father." [They said to him, "What if they were] both poor?"

One who set aside an issar and ate [food worth] half its value on account of it, and then went to another place and behold, it (i.e., the issar) came out to [the value of] a pundion (the equivalent of two issars) (Maaser Sheni 4:8): He may eat another issar's worth on account of it. One who sets aside a pundion and he ate [food worth] half its value on account of it, and then went to another place and behold, it came out to an issar, he may eat half an issar's worth on its account. This is the general rule: Before one has redeemed [second tithe], whatever increases [in value], the increase is [calculated] according to the proportion, and whatever decreases in value, the decrease is [calculated] according to the proportion. Once it has been redeemed, whatever increases [in value], the increase belongs to second [tithe], and whatever decreases, the decrease belongs to second [tithe].

5.text: One who says to his children, even if you are dying, do not touch this corner-shelf (זוית), [and] they went and found coins there -- behold, these are [considered] unconsecrated. [If] they saw their father hiding coins in a chest, in an ark, or in a cupboard, and he said, "These belong to so-and-so," [or] "These are second tithe," if [he said it] like those who deceive (e.g., the coins actually were his or were unconsecrated), he has said nothing. [But] if [he said it] like one who intends to testify, his words stand. [If] someone said to them, "I saw your father hiding [coins] in a chest, in an ark, or in a cupboard," [his words are treated like] he has said nothing. "In such-and-such a place," [or] "In such-and-such a field*שדה not שידה ("chest")," his words stand. This is the general rule: Whatever is accessible [only] to them (i.e., the descendants), he has said nothing, [and] whatever is not accessible [only] to them, his words stand.*In other words, in the first case, the witness's testimony is not accepted because he lacked the ability take the coins for himself, as they were hidden in the father's house, but in the second case, he is believed, since he presumably could have taken the coins from the field or another outside location (see Sanh. 30a:6-8).
